statement: For a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights, Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path distance dist[v] from a given source node to every other node v by maintaining the invariant that dist[v] is minimal for all visited nodes and dist[u] is minimal through visited paths for unvisited nodes.

symbols.meaning: input graph consisting of vertices and weighted edges
designated source vertex from which shortest paths are computed
distance label representing the shortest or tentative distance from source to vertex v
predecessor of vertex v on the shortest path from source
min-priority queue storing vertices keyed by tentative distance dist[·]
vertex extracted from Q having the minimum tentative distance
unvisited node or predecessor node on an alternate candidate path
number of visited nodes in the induction hypothesis

steps.text: State the induction invariant: for each visited node v, dist[v] is the shortest distance from source to v; for each unvisited node u, dist[u] is the shortest distance from source to u when traveling via visited nodes only, or infinity if no such path exists.

Base case (k = 1 visited node): The only visited node is source, with dist[source] = 0. Since negative edge weights are not allowed, 0 is the shortest possible distance to source, and the induction hypothesis holds.

Inductive step setup: Assume the invariant holds for k visited nodes. Let u be the next node selected for visiting by extracting the vertex from priority queue Q with minimum dist[u]. The claim is that dist[u] is the true shortest distance from source to u.

Formulate proof by contradiction: Suppose a shorter path from source to u exists with total cost strictly less than dist[u]. This alternative shorter path either contains another unvisited node or consists only of visited nodes prior to u.

Case 1 (shorter path contains another unvisited node): Let w be the first unvisited node on this shorter path. By induction, the subpath from source to w through visited nodes only has cost dist[w]. The cost of the path to u via w is at least dist[w] plus the minimal cost of going from w to u. Because edge costs are positive, the minimal cost from w to u is positive, meaning dist[w] + (positive number) < dist[u], implying dist[w] < dist[u]. However, u was extracted from the priority queue with minimum distance, so dist[u] <= dist[w], which is a contradiction.

Case 2 (shorter path contains no other unvisited node): Let w be the last but one node on the shortest path, which is necessarily a visited node. That implies dist[w] + Graph.Distance(w, u) < dist[u]. This is a contradiction because by the time w was visited, edge relaxation set dist[u] to at most dist[w] + Graph.Distance(w, u).

Inductive maintenance and conclusion: For all other visited nodes v, dist[v] remains the known shortest distance. For each unvisited node w, relaxing outgoing edges (u, w) via alt = dist[u] + Graph.Distance(u, w) maintains that dist[w] is the shortest distance through visited nodes. After all nodes are visited, the shortest path from source to any node v consists only of visited nodes, hence dist[v] is the true shortest distance.

assumptions.assumption: Edge weights are non-negative (strictly positive for the contradiction step in the induction)
assumptions.breaks_when: The graph contains negative edge weights or negative cycles, which invalidates the greedy step dist[u] <= dist[w] + cost(w, u)

failure_modes.signature: Computed dist values fail to equal the true shortest path distance
failure_modes.cause: Greedy choice assumption that visited nodes have finalized minimal distances is broken when negative edges allow later path extensions to reduce cost

failure_modes.signature: Returned path between source and target is suboptimal
failure_modes.cause: Halting search as soon as forward and backward frontiers touch rather than checking whether the sum of minimum priorities in both queues is at least the best full path length μ
